QuantumMechanics/en/579.response:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf T &\equiv \sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf t_i, 
\\[4pt]
\mathbf T^{2}&=\Big(\sum_{i}\mathbf t_i\Big)^{2}
            =\sum_{i}\mathbf t_i^{\,2}+2\sum_{i>j}\mathbf t_i\!\cdot\!\mathbf t_j .
\end{aligned}
\]

For each nucleon \(\mathbf t_i\) is a spin‑\(\tfrac12\) isospin operator,
\(\mathbf t_i=\tfrac12\boldsymbol{\sigma}_i\); therefore  

\[
\mathbf t_i^{\,2}= \frac14\,\boldsymbol{\sigma}_i^{\,2}= \frac14 (3\mathbf 1)=\frac34 .
\]

Hence \(\displaystyle\sum_{i}\mathbf t_i^{\,2}= \frac34\,N\).

The eigenvalue of \(\mathbf T^{2}\) on a state of total isospin quantum number
\(T\) is \(T(T+1)\) (we set \(\hbar=1\)).  Substituting the above results,

\[
T(T+1)=\frac34 N+2\sum_{i>j}\mathbf t_i\!\cdot\!\mathbf t_j .
\]

Solving for the pairwise scalar product sum gives  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\sum_{i>j} t_{i}\!\cdot\! t_{j}= \frac12\Big[T(T+1)-\frac34\,N\Big] } .
\]

Thus the required identity is proved.

TheoreticalMechanics/en/49.response:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Turning point: }A=\frac{E}{F},\\[4pt]
&\text{Period (for fixed }F):\qquad 
T =4\int_{0}^{A}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{2(E-Fx)/m}}
   =\frac{4\sqrt{2mE}}{F}=4\sqrt{\frac{2mA}{F}}\,. 
\end{aligned}
\]

For a slow (adiabatic) change of the slope \(F(t)\) the action  

\[
I=\oint p\,dx
   =\frac{4}{3}\sqrt{2m}\,\frac{E^{3/2}}{F}
\]

remains invariant \((I=\text{const})\).  Hence  

\[
\frac{E^{3/2}}{F}=\text{const}\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
E\propto F^{2/3},\qquad 
A=\frac{E}{F}\propto F^{-1/3},\qquad 
T=\frac{4\sqrt{2mE}}{F}\propto F^{-2/3}.
\]

Introducing an initial reference force \(F_{0}\) with corresponding
values \(E_{0},A_{0},T_{0}\),

\[
\boxed{%
E(F)=E_{0}\Big(\frac{F}{F_{0}}\Big)^{2/3},\qquad
A(F)=A_{0}\Big(\frac{F}{F_{0}}\Big)^{-1/3},\qquad
T(F)=T_{0}\Big(\frac{F}{F_{0}}\Big)^{-2/3}
}
\]

Thus, as the slope \(F\) increases slowly, the particle’s energy grows
as \(F^{2/3}\), its oscillation amplitude shrinks as \(F^{-1/3}\), and
its period shortens as \(F^{-2/3}\); the opposite occurs when \(F\)
decreases.

\\[2pt]

    \pi , & n_{2}>n_{1}\;( \pi\ \text{phase reversal}),
  \end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\]

so that the field in medium 1 is the sum of the incident and reflected harmonic waves (the reflected‐wave amplitude is \(\sqrt{\rho}\,E_{0}\) and its phase is \(\phi\)).  

The time‑averaged square of the field (proportional to the intensity) is

\[
\boxed{
\big\langle E^{2}(z)\big\rangle
   =\frac{E_{0}^{2}}{2}\,(1+\rho)\;+\;E_{0}^{2}\sqrt{\rho}\,
     \cos\!\big(2k_{1}z-\phi\big)
}
\]

From this expression the extremal points follow directly:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Maximum:}&\qquad\cos (2k_{1}z-\phi)=+1
   \;\Longrightarrow\;
   z_{\max}= \frac{\phi}{2k_{1}}+m\,\frac{\pi}{k_{1}}
   =\frac{\lambda_{1}}{2}\Big(m+\frac{\phi}{2\pi}\Big) ,
\\[4pt]
\text{Minimum:}&\qquad\cos (2k_{1}z-\phi)=-1
   \;\Longrightarrow\;
   z_{\min}= \frac{\phi}{2k_{1}}+\Big(m+\tfrac12\Big)
             \frac{\pi}{k_{1}}
   =\frac{\lambda_{1}}{2}\Big(m+\tfrac12+\frac{\phi}{2\pi}\Big) ,
\end{aligned}
\qquad m\in\mathbb Z,
\]

where \(\lambda_{1}=c/(n_{1}v)\) is the wavelength in medium 1.

Hence

* for \(n_{2}<n_{1}\;( \phi=0)\):
  \[
  z_{\max}=m\frac{\lambda_{1}}{2},\qquad 
  z_{\min}=\Big(m+\tfrac12\Big)\frac{\lambda_{1}}{2};
  \]

* for \(n_{2}>n_{1}\;( \phi=\pi)\):
  \[
  z_{\max}=\Big(m+\tfrac12\Big)\frac{\lambda_{1}}{2},\qquad 
  z_{\min}=m\frac{\lambda_{1}}{2}.
  \]

These are the positions of the antinodes (maximum \(\langle E^{2}\rangle\)) and nodes (minimum \(\langle E^{2}\rangle\)) of the standing‑wave pattern formed by the incident and reflected waves.

TheoreticalMechanics/en/206.response:
\[
\boxed{\;
r^{2}(\theta)=\frac{\ell^{2}}
{1+\displaystyle\sqrt{1+2E\ell^{2}}\;\cos\!\big[2(\theta-\theta_{0})\big]}\,,\qquad 
(q_{1},q_{2})=(r\cos\theta,\;r\sin\theta)
\;}
\]

*Derivation.*  
The time‑independent Hamilton–Jacobi equation  

\[
H\Big(q_{i},\frac{\partial W}{\partial q_{i}}\Big)=E
\]

with  

\[
H=\frac{p_{1}^{2}+p_{2}^{2}}{2\,(q_{1}^{2}+q_{2}^{2})}
+\frac{1}{q_{1}^{2}+q_{2}^{2}}
\]

is separable in polar variables \(r=\sqrt{q_{1}^{2}+q_{2}^{2}},\;\theta=\arctan(q_{2}/q_{1})\).  
Writing \(p_{r}=\partial W/\partial r,\;p_{\theta}=\partial W/\partial\theta\),

\[
\frac{p_{r}^{2}}{2r^{2}}+\frac{p_{\theta}^{2}}{2r^{4}}+\frac{1}{r^{2}}=E .
\]

Because \(H\) is \(\theta\)–independent, \(p_{\theta}\equiv\ell\) is a constant.
Thus

\[
p_{r}^{2}=2Er^{2}-\frac{\ell^{2}}{r^{2}}-2 ,
\qquad 
\dot r=\frac{p_{r}}{r^{2}},\qquad 
\dot\theta=\frac{\ell}{r^{4}} .
\]

Eliminating \(t\),

\[
\frac{d\theta}{dr}=
\frac{\ell}{r^{2}\sqrt{2Er^{2}-\ell^{2}/r^{2}-2}}
=\frac{\ell}{r\sqrt{2Er^{4}-2r^{2}-\ell^{2}}}\, .
\]

With the substitution \(u=r^{2}\) and then \(z=1/u\) the integral becomes elementary:

\[
\theta-\theta_{0}= -\frac12
\arcsin\!\Bigl(
\frac{\ell\bigl(z+\ell^{-2}\bigr)}{\sqrt{\ell^{-2}+2E}}
\Bigr)\!,
\qquad z=\frac1{r^{2}} .
\]

Solving for \(r\) yields the orbit equation quoted above,
with the integration constants identified as the conserved energy \(E\) and angular
momentum \(\ell\) and an arbitrary phase \(\theta_{0}\).

In Cartesian coordinates the same curve reads

\[
(1+k)q_{1}^{2}+(1-k)q_{2}^{2}=\ell^{2},
\qquad 
k\equiv\sqrt{1+2E\ell^{2}} ,
\]

i.e. a conic (ellipse for \(|k|<1\), hyperbola for \(|k|>1\)) whose shape is fixed by
\(E\) and \(\ell\). The parametric solution is \(\bigl(q_{1}(t),q_{2}(t)\bigr)
=(r(t)\cos\theta(t),\,r(t)\sin\theta(t))\) with \(r(t)\) and \(\theta(t)\) obtained
from the quadratures

\[
t-t_{0}= \int\! \frac{r^{2}\,dr}{\sqrt{2Er^{2}-\ell^{2}/r^{2}-2}},\qquad 
\theta-\theta_{0}= \int\! \frac{\ell\,dr}{r^{2}\sqrt{2Er^{2}-\ell^{2}/r^{2}-2}} .
\]

These integrals lead to the closed form expression for the orbit given in the
boxed result.
